#### 1. maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 2  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.784)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-170822, Reactome:R-HSA-9615017, Reactome:R-HSA-210745, Reactome:R-HSA-5619073, Reactome:R-HSA-5619107)

**Proposed mechanism:** KCNJ11 (HGNC:6306) —DISRUPTS→ ATP-sensitive potassium channel activity (GO:0005276); ATP-sensitive potassium channel activity (GO:0005276) —LEADS_TO→ Abnormal insulin secretion (HP:0011058); ATP-sensitive potassium channel activity (GO:0005276) —LEADS_TO→ Hyperinsulinism (HP:0000834); Abnormal insulin secretion (HP:0011058) —LEADS_TO→ Diabetes mellitus (HP:0000835); Hyperinsulinism (HP:0000834) —LEADS_TO→ Diabetes mellitus (HP:0000835). Loss-of-function mutations in KCNJ11 disrupt ATP-sensitive potassium channel activity, leading to abnormal insulin secretion and hyperinsulinism (islet cell adenomatosis) and also contributing to diabetes mellitus (MODY2).

**How to falsify it:** Discovery of pathogenic loss-of-function variants in KCNJ11 in individuals with islet cell adenomatosis or MODY2 that do not affect ATP-sensitive potassium channel activity or insulin secretion would falsify this hypothesis. Additionally, identification of distinct causal genes with no overlap in affected pathways or phenotypes would weaken this proposed link. _(variant: High frequency (>1%) of pathogenic loss-of-function variants in KCNJ11 in the general population as observed in gnomAD.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of KCNJ11 in these conditions could lead to the development of targeted therapies for both islet cell adenomatosis and MODY2, potentially involving drugs that modulate KCNJ11 activity or downstream signaling pathways. This could also improve diagnostic strategies by prioritizing KCNJ11 sequencing in patients presenting with features of either disease.

#### 3. type 2 diabetes mellitus  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.734)

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of GCK in both monogenic forms of diabetes (MODY4) and type 2 diabetes mellitus highlights GCK as a potential therapeutic target. Modulating GCK activity or downstream pathways could offer novel treatment strategies for a spectrum of glucose metabolism disorders.
